newsitem.title: USA: Rising rivers, ice jams threaten northern plains.
newsitem.headline: Rising rivers, ice jams threaten northern plains.

text.p: Thousands of volunteers piled sandbags on Tuesday in a desperate effort to hold off rising rivers across the flood-ravaged northern plains.
Record-low temperatures for April created dangerous ice jams on swollen waterways and froze floodwaters around and inside cars, homes and anything else caught in the ice.
In Wahpeton, a city of 10,000 about 50 miles (80 km) south of Fargo, residents scrambled to plug gaps in dikes that were purposely breached to allow trapped floodwaters to flow out.
"An ice jam backing up the Boix de Sioux (River) dislodged and we're waiting for the water to hit," said Barbara Cole in Waphpeton.

Similar dike repair efforts were made across the region, with the town of Appleton, Minnesota, rescued from the cresting Pomme de Terre River. A floating wooden crate damaged the town's sandbag dike late on Monday and hundreds of volunteers answered the call to repair the breach.

"They put out a call over four to five counties. There were 300 people from the (surrounding) county alone and we even had a busload of kids that came in from Minneapolis," a spokesman at the Swift County Sheriff's office said. "The threat has tapered off a bit," he added.
But some residents were not so fortunate. Several towns and isolated farmhouses had to be evacuated with the aid of helicopters and military vehicles after becoming surrounded by the floodwaters.

Ada, Minnesota, northwest of Fargo, was deserted after an emergency evacuation on Monday. A sign hung on the garage of an inundated home in Bruce, North Dakota, read "Parking reserved for fishermen only."

Thousands of people across the two states remained without electricity or heat after high-voltage towers were toppled by a powerful weekend storm whipped by strong winds. Repairs may take weeks, authorities warned.
Several people suffered carbon monoxide poisoning from trying to heat their unvented homes with portable generators.

A man in Lankin, North Dakota, was discovered frozen a short distance away from his stranded pickup truck after he apparently tried to go for help during the height of the storm on Saturday. A boy died in a housefire in Lisbon, North Dakota, when lighted candles apparently overturned in the home, which lacked electricity.

Students at North Dakota State University in Fargo were excused from class to help fill and stack sandbags along the city's temporary dikes, which authorities said needed to be raised one foot (0.3 m).

The adjacent Red River was rising fast and expected to crest over the weekend at around 38 feet (12 m), which was 20 feet (6 m) above flood stage and another 5 feet (1.5 m) higher than its level of 33 feet (10 m) Tuesday morning.

"The university requested that instructors be understanding and lenient in allowing students to go help in the sandbagging effort," geology professor Don Schwert said. "I'm going out myself. I have flood problems of my own, but so many people are out there."

City workers finishing the cleanup from the snow and ice storm then resumed flood preparations. Temperatures were around 20 degrees (-7 Celsius) with sunny skies but were expected to dip to around zero (-18 C) overnight and set records for the date across North Dakota and Minnesota.
Cool weather was forecast to continue through the week, slowing the spring thaw and possibly easing the flooding.

North and South Dakota were granted disaster declarations by President Bill Clinton on Monday and Minnesota was likely to receive federal aid as well. The Dakotas were also declared disaster areas in January following record-breaking snowstorms, and North Dakota has received similar declarations in each of the past four years because of flooding.
